_Hélène Vincent is head of performance marketing at ManyPets, formerly known as Bought By Many. Kerry Hughes oversees Performance Max campaigns for the fast-growing pet insurance company._

If you’ve bought a new pet recently, you’re not alone. Since the start of the pandemic, [3.2 million households](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-56362987) in the U.K. have done so — and many of those new owners are from a younger generation that manages their financial and [insurance needs](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/intl/en-emea/consumer-insights/consumer-journey/the-future-of-insurance-3-ways-to-engage-todays-digital-consumer/) largely online.

At [ManyPets](https://manypets.com/uk/), formerly known as Bought By Many, we’re digitising every step of the [customer journey](https://business.google.com/uk/think/consumer-insights/google-search-youtube-easier-shopping/) with the aim of making the pet insurance experience better for everyone. We’ve [grown rapidly](https://insurtechdigital.com/insurtech/timeline-bought-many), but we know there’s still plenty of demand out there – it’s estimated by Association of British Insurers that only 45% of U.K. cat and dog owners currently [hold insurance policies](https://boughtbymany.com/news/article/18-million-pet-insurance-claims-paid-out-every-day/) for their pets.

As a business, we don’t want to miss any opportunities for growth, so we’re always keen to explore and test new advertising formats and technology. Last year, we embarked on a test of fully automated [Performance Max](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/10724817?hl=en) campaigns. Here, we share the results and our three key lessons.

> With Performance Max we’re able to use different channels to engage with users at various stages of the funnel.

### More growth without adding complexity

Online visibility is paramount for discovery and brand awareness in the pet insurance sector, as it is in many others. We wanted to acquire — and retain — as many relevant consumers as we could at the best possible cost.

Previously, we’d focused on Search and YouTube as our main platforms for growth, but we wanted to diversify to other performance channels. This was to ensure we were ready to capture demand when and wherever it showed up. If we weren’t present, we knew our competitors certainly would be.

Manual solutions and siloed campaigns didn’t fit with these ambitions, putting too much demand on the team’s time and reducing the agility we needed for [international growth](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/intl/en-emea/consumer-insights/consumer-trends/uk-retailers-e-commerce-festive-season/). The main appeal of opting for Performance Max campaigns was having access to an extensive [ads inventory](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1752334) from a single automated campaign, all optimised to our conversion goals.

### Switching from siloed campaigns to a multi-channel strategy

From awareness all the way through to retargeting, with Performance Max we’re able to use different channels to engage with users at various stages of the funnel.

We upload our creative assets, set our conversion goals — in our case cost per acquisition (CPA) — then let the machine-learning perform and acquire customers. # Google LSAs vs PPC for Vets

August 7, 2026June 27, 2026 by [TailWerks](https://tailwerks.com/author/tailwerks-team/ "View all posts by TailWerks")

## Google LSAs vs PPC for Vets

Veterinary clinics compare Google Local Service Ads and traditional PPC because both can put the clinic in front of pet owners who need care. The difference is control. Local Service Ads can be useful for high-intent calls, but traditional Google Ads usually gives the clinic more control over keywords, landing pages, conversion tracking, budget allocation, and lead quality.

The better ROI comes from matching the channel to the clinic’s real constraint. If your clinic needs immediate calls and can answer them well, LSA may help. If you need to shape demand by service, location, schedule, and lead quality, traditional PPC usually gives you more room to optimize.

## What Are Google Local Service Ads for Veterinary Clinics?

Google Local Service Ads are a call-focused ad format that can appear near the top of local search results. For clinics, the appeal is simple: pet owners see a local provider, tap to call, and the clinic pays around the lead interaction rather than the click.

That simplicity is useful, but it also limits strategy. LSA does not give the same keyword-level control, landing-page testing, audience shaping, or service-specific messaging that traditional PPC provides. A clinic may receive calls, but still struggle to know which services, terms, or locations are producing the best appointments.

## What Is Traditional PPC for Veterinary Clinics?

Traditional PPC usually means Google Search campaigns built around keywords, ad groups, landing pages, negative keywords, conversion tracking, and budget control. It lets a clinic separate urgent care searches from wellness exams, dental searches, spay and neuter searches, specialty care, or new-patient intent.

This matters because not every veterinary lead has the same value or urgency. A generic click is not the goal. The goal is a qualified call, form fill, or appointment request from a pet owner the clinic can actually serve.

## Where Local Service Ads Usually Win

LSA can work well when the clinic has strong phone coverage, a clear service area, and demand that converts quickly by phone. It can also help when a clinic wants to test local paid visibility without building a full search campaign first.

*   High-intent local calls
*   Simple service categories
*   Fast setup compared with a full PPC build
*   Visibility near the top of some local results
*   Lead-review options that may help with obvious junk leads

## Where Traditional PPC Usually Wins

Traditional PPC wins when the clinic needs control. If you want to prioritize dental appointments, urgent care, new patients, exotics, specialty services, or a specific location, search campaigns give you the levers to do that.

*   Keyword and negative keyword control
*   Service-specific ad copy
*   Landing pages matched to the searcher’s intent
*   Better testing across offers and calls to action
*   Cleaner conversion tracking for calls, forms, and booked appointments
*   Budget control by service line or location

## ROI Depends on Lead Quality, Not Just Cost Per Lead

A cheaper lead is not better if it does not book, does not fit your services, or calls when the clinic cannot answer. Veterinary PPC ROI should be judged by qualified appointment opportunities, not just clicks, calls, or form fills.

The right comparison is not “LSA cost versus PPC cost.” It is whether each channel produces the kind of cases the clinic wants, at a volume the team can handle, with enough tracking to improve month after month.

## A Practical Decision Matrix

| Situation | Better Starting Point | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You need more immediate phone inquiries | Local Service Ads | LSA can capture simple high-intent local calls quickly. |
| You need better control by service line | Traditional PPC | Search campaigns can separate budgets, keywords, ads, and landing pages. |
| You have weak call answering | Fix operations first | Both channels waste money if good calls are missed. |
| You want to scale across multiple locations | Traditional PPC plus local SEO | Multi-location growth needs reporting, segmentation, and page-level strategy. |
| You do not know where leads are leaking | Search-to-Schedule Audit | Audit the path before adding more spend. |

## Most Clinics Should Not Treat This as Either-Or

The strongest setup often uses both. LSA can capture a slice of ready-to-call local demand while traditional PPC gives the clinic strategic control. The key is measuring both against the same business outcome: qualified booked appointments.

If LSA brings calls but PPC brings better cases, the budget should reflect that. If PPC gets traffic but the landing page confuses pet owners, the campaign is not the only problem. If both channels bring calls that go unanswered, the fix starts at the phone.

## FAQ

### Are Local Service Ads better than Google Ads for vets?

Not always. Local Service Ads can work for direct calls, but Google Ads gives more control over keywords, landing pages, budgets, and service-specific strategy.

### Should a veterinary clinic run both LSA and PPC?

Often, yes, if the clinic can track calls and lead quality. Running both can work when each channel has a clear role and budget is adjusted based on booked appointment quality.

### What should vets track before judging ROI?

Track answered calls, qualified leads, booked appointments, service type, location, and whether the inquiry fits the clinic. Clicks and raw lead counts are not enough.

# Google Ads for Veterinary Clinics: A New Client Guide

November 2, 2026

![Vasant Chaudhary](/_next/image?url=%2Fvasant.webp&w=96&q=75&dpl=dpl_7xHTkgMLFNN16qEDggk12zEHkT19)

Vasant Chaudhary

Google Ads specialist. $30M+ managed across 50+ e-commerce and agency accounts in the US, UK and India. [Book a free audit call](https://improtics.com/book-a-call)

On this page

It is 9:40 on a Tuesday night. A family moved to town three weeks ago, has not registered with a vet yet, and their spaniel has just eaten something from the kitchen bin. One of them types "emergency vet open now" into a phone. Earlier that same day, a couple who adopted a kitten typed "vet near me accepting new patients" and booked a first exam with whichever clinic answered the phone. Both searches start a relationship that can last ten years or more. Only one of them should be seeing your ad, depending on what your clinic can actually do at that hour.

**Short version:** Google Ads for veterinary clinics works when the account is built around three facts. A new client household is worth years of visits across every pet in the home, not one exam. Your capacity is set by vets, rooms and opening hours, so emergency demand and day clinic demand need different campaigns and schedules. And most pet owners call, so calls must be tracked with a sensible duration threshold and matched to new clients actually seen. The clinics that get steady results split campaigns by service line (new clients, wellness and vaccines, dental, surgery, emergency), judge cost per new client against lifetime value, run emergency ads only when someone can take the case, and keep a firm negative list for jobs, vet school and low cost clinic searches. This guide covers the structure, the math, tracking, keywords, local signals, Local Services Ads, policy and budgets.

This post is about veterinary practices: general practice clinics, animal hospitals, and the emergency and specialty hospitals that have a section of their own further down. If you sell pet food, toys and supplies online, our guide to [Google Ads for pet supply stores](https://improtics.com/blog/google-ads-for-pet-supply-stores) is the one you want. Many clinics sell food and medication too, but the advertising problem for a clinic is filling appointment slots, not shipping orders.

## Why Google Ads for veterinary clinics works

Pet owners rarely browse for a vet. They search when they need one: a new puppy needs vaccines, a cat has stopped eating, a family has moved, or their current clinic cannot see them for two weeks. That search is the moment they choose, and many choose from the first page of results, often the map pack and the ads above it. Search ads put your clinic in front of that decision with your hours, distance and phone number in view.

The economics suit paid search too. A client who stays brings every pet in the household to you for wellness visits, vaccines, dental work, sick visits and, in time, surgery and senior care. That gives a clinic room to pay a real cost per click for the right searches, as long as the account measures new clients seen rather than clicks or raw calls. Veterinary marketing that only counts phone rings will always look better or worse than it is.

Volume is also steady. Pets get sick all year, puppies and kittens arrive all year, and vaccine reminders run on a cycle. There are seasonal bumps (parasite season, holiday food incidents, the weeks after people adopt), but a vet clinic does not live or die on one quarter the way a gift store does. That makes it easier to learn from the data month by month.

## Day clinic or emergency hospital: two different accounts

The first decision in Google Ads for veterinary clinics is what kind of practice you are advertising, because a general practice and an emergency hospital want very different searches.

General practice day clinic

*   Wants new client households and planned care
*   Searches like "vet near me", "puppy vaccines", "dog dental cleaning"
*   Value comes from years of visits across pets
*   Ads run in and just before opening hours
*   Judge on cost per new client seen

Emergency or 24 hour hospital

*   Wants urgent cases it can treat tonight
*   Searches like "emergency vet open now", "24 hour vet"
*   Value comes from the case itself, often a high invoice
*   Ads run when the hospital is open and staffed
*   Judge on cost per case seen, with calls as the main signal

Many day clinics offer urgent same day appointments during opening hours. That is worth advertising, honestly worded, but it is not an emergency service, and an ad that says "emergency vet" at 10 at night when nobody will answer the phone wastes money and frustrates a frightened owner. Keep the two intents in separate campaigns so each has its own schedule, ads and budget.

## Campaign structure for vet clinic Google Ads

A veterinary practice does not sell one service. Wellness care, dental, surgery and urgent care attract different searches, have different invoice sizes and use different parts of the diary. One "veterinarian" campaign forces one budget and one set of ads across all of them and hides which service lines bring in new clients.

| Campaign | Purpose | Why it is separate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brand Search | Your clinic name and individual vet names | Cheap, protects existing clients and referrals from competitors bidding on your name |
| New client and near me | "Vet near me", "veterinarian \[town\]", "new patient vet" | Highest intent in the account, deserves protected budget |
| Wellness and vaccines | Puppy and kitten care, vaccinations, wellness plans | Steady volume that starts a long relationship |
| Dental | Pet dental cleaning, dental exams, extractions | Higher invoice, booked ahead, fills dental days |
| Surgery and spay and neuter | Spay, neuter, lump removal, soft tissue surgery | Price shoppers and low cost clinics compete here |
| Emergency and urgent care | "Emergency vet", "urgent vet", "after hours vet" | Runs only when you can take the case |
| Exotics (only if offered) | Rabbits, birds, reptiles, small mammals | Low competition, small volume, very specific owners |

![Google Ads campaign structure for veterinary clinics: Brand Search, New client and near me, Wellness and vaccines, Dental, Surgery and spay and neuter, Emergency and urgent care, and Exotics](/diagrams/google-ads-for-veterinary-clinics-campaign-structure.svg)

A clean veterinary account gives each service line its own campaign and runs emergency ads on their own schedule.

Smaller clinics do not need all seven on day one. A sensible start is Brand, New client and near me, and one service campaign for whatever has the most
